section_summary: This section continues a Spanish-language economic study of the Great Depression, concluding a discussion of agricultural and industrial unemployment with comparative figures for Germany, the United States, Great Britain, and Japan. It then opens a chapter on international trade, documenting the contraction of world commerce after 1929 and attributing it to falling purchasing power, monetary disorder, trade barriers, industrial redistribution, and the policies of major industrial countries. The final pages compare industrial growth among regions and begin Octavio Morató’s classification of countries by stages of economic development.

people.name: Octavio Morató
people.role: Cited commentator who classifies countries according to four stages of economic development.

subfiles.title: Economic study of unemployment and international trade
subfiles.about: An economic analysis of Depression-era unemployment, the collapse of international trade, and the geographic redistribution of industry.
subfiles.summary: The excerpt concludes a discussion of unemployment by tracing agricultural joblessness to wartime expansion of grain cultivation, the recovery of European agriculture, mechanization, falling prices, and migration into cities. A comparative table presents unemployment figures for Germany, the United States, Great Britain, and Japan. A new chapter charts the sharp decline in world imports and exports after 1929 and identifies falling purchasing power, monetary disruption, tariff barriers, industrial redistribution, and misguided commercial policy as causes. It compares the pace of industrial development across European and non-European regions and begins Octavio Morató’s four-stage model of economic development.
